title: Terahertz anomalous Hall effect in magnetic Weyl semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
authors: Ashutosh Singh, Hongjing Xu, Xielin Wang, Kohei Fujiwara, Atsushi Tsukazaki, Shengxi Huang, Andrey Baydin, Junichiro Kono, Alexey Belyanin
abstract: Time-reversal-symmetry-broken Weyl semimetals are known to have at least two nodes in their electronic band structure, separated in momentum space and acting as sources and sinks of Berry curvature. This gives rise to a transverse Hall conductivity, known as the anomalous Hall effect (AHE), which, in the simplest two-node picture, is proportional to the momentum-space separation between the nodes in the zero frequency limit. In the recently discovered Weyl semimetal $\mathrm{Co_3Sn_2S_2}$, a giant AHE has been observed. However, experimental investigations in the low-energy regime, which directly probe quasiparticle excitations near the Weyl nodes, remain limited. Here, we present a systematic study of the intrinsic low-energy gyrotropic optical response of $\mathrm{Co_3Sn_2S_2}$ using terahertz spectroscopy combined with semianalytical calculations based on a physically intuitive effective model. Our results provide a robust and transparent explanation of the observed magnetooptical phenomena in terms of intrinsic gyrotropy arising from momentum-space separation of the Weyl nodes. Furthermore, quantitative comparison between experiment and theory places stringent constraints on the material parameters.
summary: This work systematically analyzes the Terahertz anomalous Hall effect in the Weyl semimetal $	ext{Co}_3	ext{Sn}_2	ext{S}_2$. By developing an effective low-energy model Hamiltonian, the authors calculate the intrinsic optical conductivity components ($\sigma_{xx}$ and $\sigma_{xy}$). The theoretical results provide a robust explanation for the observed magneto-optical behavior by linking it directly to the momentum-space separation of the Weyl nodes.
main_problem: The study investigates the Terahertz anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in the magnetic Weyl semimetal $	ext{Co}_3	ext{Sn}_2	ext{S}_2$ by linking its intrinsic optical response to the momentum-space separation of its Weyl nodes.
main_result: The theoretical model successfully reproduces the measured magneto-optical phenomena, explaining the longitudinal and transverse conductivity signatures in the THz range via intrinsic gyrotropy.
method: The authors employ the Kubo formalism to calculate optical conductivity ($\sigma_{xx}, \sigma_{xy}$) using a minimal two-band effective Hamiltonian, comparing these calculations against THz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) measurements.
model_or_system: The system is the magnetic Weyl semimetal $	ext{Co}_3	ext{Sn}_2	ext{S}_2$. The analysis uses a minimal two-band model Hamiltonian describing the electronic structure near the Weyl nodes, which exhibit Berry curvature sources and sinks.
key_observables: Longitudinal conductivity ($	ext{Re}[\sigma_{xx}]$), transverse (Hall) conductivity ($	ext{Re}[\sigma_{xy}]$), and the Faraday rotation angle ($	ext{Re}[\Theta_F]$) in the THz frequency range.
important_parameters: Momentum-space separation ($Q$) between Weyl nodes, chemical potential ($\mu$), and the energy parameter $b$ derived from the material structure.
main_assumptions: Key approximations include neglecting interband transitions ($\hbar\omega \ll \mu$) and assuming an effective low-energy model based on the two-node picture.
figures_summary: Figures compare measured $	ext{Re}[\sigma_{xx}]$ vs. temperature with model calculations, show $	ext{Re}[\sigma_{xy}]$ saturation, and illustrate the temperature dependence of the chemical potential.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical basis of AHE in Weyl semimetals, develops a minimal effective Hamiltonian, calculates the optical conductivity components ($\sigma_{xx}, \sigma_{xy}$) using the Kubo formula, and finally compares these theoretical predictions with experimental THz-TDS data.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter physics, the use of linear response theory (Kubo formalism) to model optical response and the explicit connection between band topology (Weyl nodes) and macroscopic transport properties (AHE) are relevant concepts in open quantum systems and quantum optics.
